channel.title: Responsible AI & Neurodivergence, Naba Rizvi
channel.description: Daily curated research feed on ethical and responsible AI, with emphasis on neurodivergent people and serious mental illness.

item.title: How LLMs Respond to Escalating Delusions: Four Longitudinal Trajectories of Model Behavior
item.description: Fifteen widely used models were prompted across 30 days with the same 30 message script, tracing a progression from mild anomalous experiences through to frank psychotic ideation, which makes this a longitudinal safety assessment rather than a single turn probe. Four distinct response trajectories emerged: premature medicalisation and disengagement, recognition without safeguarding where the model offers itself as sufficient help, delayed and unstable recognition that arrives late and fails to build, and active co construction of delusional content. The trajectories cut across vendors rather than sorting neatly by lab or model size, which suggests the behaviour follows from training objectives shared across the field. The framing of iatrogenic harm is the useful contribution, since it puts the question in clinical terms: what does sustained exposure to this system do to someone already moving toward psychosis.

item.title: Auditing Stealth Sycophancy in Mental Health Dialogue: Structured Clinical State Diagnostics and Clean Matched Benchmarks
item.description: The target here is implicit sycophancy, a failure mode where a reply reads as warm and supportive while quietly reinforcing catastrophising, avoidance, hopeless prediction or premature CBT style labelling. That matters because automated evaluators routinely treat surface empathy, supportiveness and fluency as evidence of safety, so the evaluator and the failure share the same blind spot. The authors build a diagnostic benchmark from everyday peer support, counselling style emotional support and crisis oriented interaction, plus a leakage audited matched set of 500 contexts and 1,500 response windows, then propose an evaluator that scores decoupled clinical states by direction of movement rather than by tone. The design point generalises beyond this paper: safety scoring has to ask where the conversation is heading, not how kind it sounds.

item.title: Potentially Harmful Consequences of AI Chatbot Use Among Patients With Mental Illness: Early Data From a Large Psychiatric Service System
item.description: Most of the AI psychosis literature runs on simulation, case reports or platform disclosures, so this counts as a different kind of evidence: a search of records from the Psychiatric Services of the Central Denmark Region, covering roughly 1.4 million inhabitants, across the period from September 2022 to June 2025. The authors looked for documented instances compatible with chatbot use contributing to the onset or worsening of delusions or mania, particularly where interaction was intense or sustained. Grounding the phenomenon in routine clinical documentation moves the question from whether anecdotes exist to how often services actually encounter this, which is what prevalence arguments have been missing. It also establishes a method that other health systems can replicate on their own records.

item.title: A Shift in Trust: An Analysis of the Use of AI Chatbots Among People Living With Bipolar Disorder
item.description: Semi structured interviews with two people diagnosed with bipolar disorder who had independently adopted ChatGPT for self reflection, diagnostic exploration, symptom management and treatment questions. Both described the tool as versatile and genuinely useful, offering educational, emotional and social support, and both described their use migrating from information seeking toward personal and relational functions over time. That drift is the finding worth carrying forward, since the risks of overreliance and displaced clinical trust attach to the relational mode rather than the informational one. The sample is two people and the authors present it as preliminary, but qualitative depth on serious mental illness specifically is scarce enough that it fills a real gap.

item.title: When Markets Shape AI Mental Health Self Management Tools: Consequences for Serious Mental Illness
item.description: Health policy increasingly folds AI enabled self management tools into digital models of mental health care, but the authors point out that development follows commercial logic rather than clinical need. Investment concentrates on scalable, low intensity interventions for anxiety and depression, while schizophrenia spectrum and bipolar populations remain comparatively underserved despite carrying a disproportionate share of morbidity and service use. The argument reframes an equity problem that is usually described as a data gap or a recruitment failure, locating the absence instead in something structural and economic, produced by where the addressable market sits. That reframing matters for remedies, since better datasets will not fix an incentive that never pointed at these populations.

item.title: A transdiagnostic model for how general purpose AI chatbots can perpetuate OCD and anxiety disorders
item.description: The paper applies a transdiagnostic CBT informed framework to name the specific mechanism by which general purpose chatbots can entrench OCD and anxiety, which is negative reinforcement of avoidance. Reassurance seeking gets answered, uncertainty gets resolved on demand, and the corrective learning that exposure would produce never happens, so intolerance of uncertainty, need to know compulsions and perfectionism are fed rather than challenged. The authors add a perceptual wrinkle, noting that when a model draws on earlier turns and replies in personally relevant terms, users read this as being understood, when what it reflects is retrieval and recombination of context. Recommendations are split across clinicians, users, developers and policymakers, which is the right division given that no single actor controls the reinforcement loop.

item.title: Evaluation of AI generated vignettes depicting patient chatbot use in psychiatric contexts
item.description: A proof of concept study asking whether a frontier model can write usable teaching material about the clinical problem it is itself implicated in. Three board certified psychiatrists rated ChatGPT 5 Pro vignettes on chatbot relevance, diagnostic sufficiency, quality of explanation and safety. Relevance and diagnostic sufficiency scored well while safety ratings lagged, which the authors read as a requirement for expert review before any educational deployment rather than as a verdict against the approach. The underlying motivation is worth noting on its own, since trainees now need competence in recognising chatbot related mental health risk, and the teaching cases for that do not yet exist in the standard casebooks.

item.title: A scoping literature review of generative artificial intelligence for supporting neurodivergent school students
item.description: Twenty one sources drawn from academic databases and grey literature between 2020 and 2024, covering generative AI use with neurodivergent students in K 12 settings, including ADHD, autism, dyslexia, gifted and twice exceptional learners. The dominant applications cluster around personalised learning and administrative assistance, the latter meaning teacher facing work such as drafting individualised education programmes. The gaps the authors identify are practical rather than conceptual: almost no guidance on folding AI generated personalised content into existing lesson plans and curricula, and no implementation framework for the IEP use that is already happening. That combination, adoption running ahead of guidance, is the recurring shape of this literature.

item.title: Redefining communication in mental healthcare: generative AI for neurodivergent equity and non verbal autistic inclusion
item.description: The starting claim is that non verbal autistic people are underserved in mental healthcare because the dominant communicative norms of the clinic do not match their embodied and sensory modes of expression. Echolalia, rhythmic movement, gesture and sensory signalling get treated as behaviour to be managed rather than communication to be understood, and psychiatric models that privilege speech, linear reasoning and neurotypical expressivity either misclassify these attempts or drop them entirely. The authors position generative AI as a possible translation layer between those modes and clinical documentation, while insisting that the ethical conditions come first. The framing is the contribution, since it locates the deficit in the assessment apparatus rather than the patient, which is where the responsible AI question actually sits.

item.title: Governing AI for Mental Health: Fragmented State Approaches and the Case for a Federal Framework
item.description: A four state case analysis covering Illinois, Utah, New York and Nevada finds two distinct regulatory strategies in play: rules that govern the use of AI within clinical contexts, and rules that govern the technology itself, with some states blending the two. The divergence is not merely stylistic, since it produces uneven consumer protection depending on where someone lives, and leaves developers, vendors, deployers and clinicians facing genuine uncertainty about which obligations attach to them. The authors use this to argue for a federal framework, which is the live policy question now that state activity has outpaced anything at the national level. For readers tracking serious mental illness specifically, the analysis is a useful map of which protections would and would not follow a patient across state lines.
